body:
## Problem

`nvim_set_option_value('foldmethod', 'nonsense', { win = 0, dry_run = true })` succeeds, although assigning the same value fails with E474. Dry runs skip value checks embedded in the `did_set_*` callbacks.

Direct option assignments in C folding commands duplicate setter side effects. In `:retab`, they miss updates to C code indentation and folds based on indentation when tab widths change.

## Solution

Split value validation out of `did_set_*` into `validation_cb` callbacks shared by normal assignments and `nvim_set_option_value()` dry runs. Keep side effects in `did_set_*`.

Use normal setters for C folding commands and `:retab`, sharing option updates, `OptionSet` events, and fold synchronization with Lua assignments. Stop processing if `OptionSet` leaves the command's window or buffer.

`:retab` temporarily disables `'list'` to calculate tab widths. Check the argument first so an error such as `:retab -1` does not leave `'list'` disabled.

comment_data.body: why can't we reuse `optset_T`, why do we need a new struct + callback ? I guess because `did_set_xx` has side-effects... but maybe `optset_T.validate = true` could disable that. Then validation + side-effects live in 1 handler. Not sure if that's better though.

Bad AI 😬

Yeah, we could do that and it would be less churn. We would still need to mark in `options.lua` which options callbacks support validation as they would need to be called in `dry_run` with `validation_only=true`. However one of the main problems with `did_set_*` functions is they are run **after** the option has been set, so really they should be strictly for side-effects. By moving the validation before setting, we can error out earlier without having to worry about cleaning up, which is a better design IMO. I'll remove `optvalidate_T`, but it looks like it doesn't simplify code as we need to populate more fields before calling the validation callback in `validate_option_value`. So we remove a struct but add some slightly awkward (duplicated) logic.

I don't think it does save an allocation, but using this is better.

We don't actually need the third argument to `opt_keyset` (anymore?).

Replaced with:

```c
OptKeyDict_pvp *v = opt_keyset(value, kOptPreviewpopup);
```

> By moving the validation before setting, we can error out earlier without having to worry about cleaning up, which is a better design IMO.

true 👍
I meant "stack allocation" or whatever 😂
There's not even an extra stack allocation. The return value and the third argument pointer where the same.
I would mildly prefer to keep the `keyset` param so that it's not re-implemented in a worse way in the future, if/when it is needed.
What is the motivation for it? One of the outcomes of this PR is that this sort of handling is no longer required.

Ok, I think I understand now why you want this, though it's not that obvious on the surface.

Basically since `OptKeyDict` is a union, returning that by value would allocate more on the stack. Whereas using `static` limits this and make use of the fact we mainly only deal with one option at a time.

With that said this does seem a bit of a micro-op. Returning by value would allocate more on the stack, but is that much of a problem?

I'll revert the change for this PR, but given how much code we're moving to Lua where these sorts of memory consideration are given much less weight, I do think we should rethink introducing these sorts of optimizations, especially when the alternative can be all done on the stack.

> With that said this does seem a bit of a micro-op

it's a micro-op, but harmless...



> but given how much code we're moving to Lua where these sorts of memory consideration are given much less weight

Options and autocmds are an extreme hotpath. If those subsystems were fully in Lua, we would have different optimization opportunities (better use of shared dicts + weak tables, string builder, better architecture, ...). In C we can and do continue to avoid allocations where possible, if it's low-cost, which in this case it is.

It's low cost LOC-wise but a bit obscure and thus high-cost comprehension-wise, at least with my level of C skills (which isn't that high mind you, but probably above average at this point). It took me a few looks and AI to spoon feed me what this was exactly optimizing, and also introduces some potential footguns if this optimization is accidentally misused.

And again I don't think stack allocations were such a big deal (almost free?). Is this avoided heap allocations then this might be a more justified. I don't think this code-path is even re-entrant so it's not like the extra stack space can be multiplied. And one could argue local stack would be more performant on a CPU verse static storage which may have bad locality (more likely to have an L1/L2 miss).

Basically, without proper benchmarks, these sorts of optimizations are probably doing more harm than good.

> And one could argue local stack would be more performant on a CPU verse static storage which may have bad locality (more likely to have an L1/L2 miss).

Hmm... didn't think about that. Not sure if I measured the actual size of `OptKeyDict`, if it's small then yes it doesn't matter.
I'll profile, though benchmarks will probably need to be highly synthetic since I don't actually think option **setting** is that hot. Option **reading** is hot due to things like `win_line()`.

> Option **reading** is hot due to things like `win_line()`.

Yes. My assumption was that the "keyset" form could be useful in more places that read. That may turn out to be wrong though. It depends on how much remaining "cleanup" is fruitful for the options system.

I profiled this and with the current dict options and returning by value is a hair quicker. I also looked at adding a dict option that was 4kb to increase the union, and this made return by value a hair slower. And this is all in the realm is nanoseconds. Error margins probably make this a wash.
